h1: Florida HOA Records Request Letter Generator
metaTitle: Florida HOA Records Request Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate a Florida HOA records request demand letter under Fla. Stat. 720.303. Enforce your right to inspect HOA records within 10 business days.
penalty: $50 per day for up to 10 days ($500 maximum), plus actual damages and attorney's fees
introParagraph: If you live in a Florida homeowners' association, you have a legal right to inspect and copy the association's official records. Florida law gives HOAs only 10 business days to respond to a written records request, and associations that ignore or stonewall requests face statutory penalties. Many Florida homeowners run into board members or property managers who delay, redact improperly, or charge excessive fees. A properly written records request letter that cites the correct statute, identifies the records sought, and warns of penalties is often the fastest way to get compliance without filing a lawsuit. This tool generates a Florida-specific demand letter tailored to Chapter 720 so you can assert your rights clearly and create a paper trail if you later need to pursue arbitration, mediation, or court action.
lawExplanation: Florida's Homeowners' Association Act, codified at Chapter 720 of the Florida Statutes, governs records access for parcel owners in HOA-governed communities. Under Fla. Stat. § 720.303(4), the association must maintain official records including the governing documents, meeting minutes for the prior seven years, current rosters of all members and their addresses, financial reports, contracts, insurance policies, and ballots and voting records for at least one year. Section 720.303(5) requires the association to make these records available for inspection by any parcel owner or their authorized representative within 10 business days of receiving a written request, sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, or by hand delivery. The HOA must allow inspection at a reasonable place and time within the county where the community is located. Some records are exempt from inspection, including attorney-client privileged communications, information about ongoing litigation, personnel records, medical records, and Social Security numbers or other personal identifying information of owners. The association may charge reasonable copying costs but cannot impose excessive fees as a barrier to access. If the HOA willfully fails to provide access, Florida law presumes the homeowner has been damaged and entitles them to minimum statutory damages of $50 per day for each day past the 10-business-day deadline, up to 10 days ($500 cap on the daily penalty), in addition to actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. The Division of Florida Condominiums, Timeshares, and Mobile Homes within the Department of Business and Professional Regulation handles certain disputes, and pre-suit mediation is generally required for HOA disputes under Fla. Stat. § 720.311 before a lawsuit can be filed.
letterStrategy: An effective Florida HOA records request letter does three things: it clearly identifies the records sought, it cites the controlling statute, and it preserves your right to statutory damages by creating a documented start date for the 10-business-day clock. Send the letter by certified mail with return receipt requested, or deliver it in person and obtain a signed acknowledgment. List each category of records specifically rather than asking for 'all records,' which boards sometimes use as an excuse to delay. Reference Fla. Stat. § 720.303(4) and (5) so the recipient understands you know the law. State that you are willing to pay reasonable copying costs and propose dates and times to inspect originals at the association's office or another reasonable location in the county. Include language warning that willful failure to comply within 10 business days will trigger statutory damages of up to $500, plus actual damages and attorney's fees under § 720.303(5). Keep a copy of the letter, the certified mail receipt, and the green card or delivery confirmation. If the HOA fails to respond, partially complies, or charges unreasonable fees, your demand letter becomes critical evidence in mediation or court showing willful noncompliance. Many Florida HOAs and their property managers comply quickly once they receive a properly drafted letter because the statutory penalties and attorney's fee exposure are clear and well-established under Florida case law.
proceduralNotes: Before filing suit over an HOA records dispute in Florida, § 720.311 generally requires pre-suit mediation, and the requesting party must serve a statutory demand for mediation. Small claims actions in Florida county court have a jurisdictional limit of $8,000, exclusive of costs, interest, and attorney's fees, which is sufficient for most records-request damages claims. Filing fees in county court typically range from $55 to $300 depending on the claim amount. The statute of limitations for statutory violations under Chapter 720 is generally four or five years, but you should act promptly. Keep meticulous records of every communication. Note that condominiums (governed by Chapter 718) and cooperatives (Chapter 719) have separate but similar records-access rules with different penalty structures.

faq.q: What records can I request from my Florida HOA?
faq.a: Under Fla. Stat. § 720.303(4), you can request governing documents, meeting minutes from the past seven years, member rosters, financial statements and audits, contracts, insurance policies, budgets, tax returns, and voting records. Some items are exempt, including attorney-client privileged communications, pending litigation strategy, personnel files, medical records, and personal identifiers like Social Security numbers. The association must keep these records within Florida and make them available for inspection at a reasonable location in the county where the community sits.

faq.q: How long does my HOA have to respond to my records request?
faq.a: Florida law gives the HOA 10 business days from receipt of your written request to make the records available for inspection. The clock starts when the association receives your certified-mail letter or hand-delivered request. Business days exclude weekends and legal holidays. If the HOA willfully fails to provide access within that window, you are entitled to statutory damages of $50 per day for up to 10 days, capped at $500, plus actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees.

faq.q: Do I have to pay for copies of HOA records?
faq.a: Yes, but only reasonable costs. The HOA can charge for the actual cost of copying and, if a person is needed to supervise inspection or retrieve records, reasonable personnel costs. However, charges cannot be so excessive that they effectively block access. You also have the right to bring your own scanner or camera to inspect originals at no cost. If your HOA imposes unreasonable fees, document them in writing and reference this practice in any follow-up demand or legal filing.

faq.q: What if my HOA still refuses after I send a demand letter?
faq.a: If the HOA ignores your letter or refuses access, your next step under Fla. Stat. § 720.311 is typically to serve a statutory demand for pre-suit mediation, which is generally required before filing a lawsuit over records disputes. You can then file in Florida county court, with small claims jurisdiction up to $8,000. You may recover statutory damages, actual damages, and attorney's fees. Some homeowners also file complaints with the Department of Business and Professional Regulation, though DBPR's HOA jurisdiction is limited compared to condominiums.

faq.q: Does the records request law apply to all Florida HOAs?
faq.a: Chapter 720 applies to mandatory homeowners' associations governing residential parcels in Florida, which covers the vast majority of single-family and townhome HOA communities. Condominium associations are governed separately by Chapter 718, and cooperatives by Chapter 719, though both have similar records-access rights with their own penalty structures. Voluntary or social associations without recorded covenants generally are not covered. If you are unsure whether your community falls under Chapter 720, check your recorded declaration of covenants and consult an attorney.
